Task models that generate interfaces. Cao, Jiang and Xia's "Generative and Malleable User Interfaces with Generative and Evolving Task-Driven Data Model" (CHI 2025) proposes a structured task-driven model between a user's request and the rendered interface. In Jelly, an LLM produces an object-relational schema and dependency graph, with data organised under that structure; UI specifications map the model to a constrained set of established display patterns. Users can modify the resulting information space by language or direct manipulation, and inspect the model rather than endlessly re-prompting an opaque layout. The technical evaluation assessed schema relevance and dependency accuracy, not the correctness of arbitrary underlying source documents. Its user study involved eight participants completing open-ended information tasks; it documented enthusiasm and flexibility, but also limits in visual expressiveness and cases where requested changes were not made. This is evidence that a task-to-model-to-interface-to-revision loop can run and be manipulated. It is not a controlled demonstration of superior task accuracy, transfer or time against a strong conventional interface, nor a demonstration that the underlying data is faithfully sourced.

This is the step most people skip. They install Pi, run a task, get something nearly right, and start writing code against a mental model built from observation. The model is usually close enough to work and wrong in a few named places, and those places are where every interesting bug lives.

Why "wrong in a few places" is worse than "wrong everywhere" is worth one sentence of its own, because it explains the shape of the rest of the book. A model that is wrong everywhere fails loudly: you stop and read the documentation. A model that is nearly right fails as a symptom. The model ignores your instructions. Your tool never appears. Your injected content vanishes after a compaction. Your handler fires at the wrong moment. Each of those observations is compatible with several different causes — some in your code, some in Pi's, some in the way you assembled the request — and the observation alone cannot tell them apart. What tells them apart is knowing the exact mechanism the symptom passed through. That mechanism is the loop.

This book is about building systems around models. Before we build planners, memory, tool routing, critics, search and verifiers, we need an answer to a question that turns out to be harder than it looks:

The word is currently applied to almost everything: a single LLM call, a chatbot, a fixed pipeline, a tool-using loop, and any five model calls with class names ending in. Those systems may all be useful. But when one word covers all of them, it stops telling us anything about the computation, and we lose the ability to say which mechanism is doing the work.

The experiment was planned carefully. Eight synthetic tasks, each built around a fact that could not be inferred from the task text alone. Each task ran under three conditions: no supplied context, a matched distractor of the same size and shape, and the exact minimal context the task needed. One model, decoding fixed, every run in its own session, deterministic graders. The question was modest: if correct context is delivered through the live runtime, does behaviour change?

Twenty-four runs were planned and twenty-four executed. None yielded a valid observation of the assigned context condition. Every run reported zero observed context records because the recording component produced none. For the intended injection conditions, that leaves delivery unverified. For the no-context controls, it leaves absence unverified: an observer that did not record the request cannot distinguish a request with no experimental block from a request it never saw.

The distinction that matters is between behavioural influence from position and policy authority. If moving an instruction changes compliance, that does not mean its authority changed. The OpenAI Model Spec dated 18 August 2026 describes an instruction hierarchy running from Root through System, Developer and User to Guideline. Authority is assigned through the instruction source and applicable policy, not by being physically closer to the answer. For instructions at the same authority level, later applicable instructions can supersede earlier conflicting ones; this is a policy rule with conditions, not a general claim that whichever text appears last wins. The specification also treats tool outputs and quoted text as untrusted by default. This is OpenAI's documented policy for its own systems, not a universal law or evidence that a model always complies. Other providers may specify different policies.

The plugin is therefore useful for two reasons.

It gives us a working application.

More importantly, it forces the architecture developed throughout this book to cross the boundary from experiment into software.

Chapter 8 showed that historical truth and current truth must coexist. "The service used SQLite in March" remains true after PostgreSQL becomes current. Deleting the SQLite history to protect current answers would improve one query by corrupting another.

Chapter 14 showed the complementary point: preserving an item does not imply seating it in the current model context. The store may contain thousands of memories. The model receives a bounded working set selected for the current goal.

These results produce a useful invariant:

That invariant suggests a conservative growth strategy. The system does not need to destroy history merely because history grows. Before irreversible deletion is considered, it can change which representations compete and under what conditions.

The chapter therefore begins with a conservative bias: preserve first, suppress reversibly, delete only for reasons stronger than convenience.

Some deployments require deletion for reasons independent of memory quality — privacy policy, legal compliance, secret rotation, or user-requested erasure. Those requirements do not establish that age or low retrieval frequency is a sound memory-decay rule.

The reliable uncertainty signal is distributional. Semantic entropy (Farquhar et al.) and self-consistency checking (Manakul et al., SelfCheckGPT) both work by comparing multiple samples rather than reading one run's logprobs, and both beat single-sequence likelihood as confabulation detectors. This is the same lesson as Chapter 21: the object worth measuring is the distribution, not the draw — and that holds for interior signals too. Be precise about what "detector" buys, though. Three capabilities pull apart: detect (this response is probably a confabulation), localize (this token or span is the wrong one), explain (this is why the weights preferred it). A multi-sample meaning-cluster signal reaches the first on QA-style tasks and no further — it does not point at the veer token, it does not name a mechanism, and it fails silently on confident fabrication, where every sample lands on the same wrong answer so the cluster entropy stays low. That is the exact sense in which interior signals never convict: good detectors exist, localizers and explainers do not, and even the good detectors have a blind spot a probe would catch. The cheap single-pass version is a hidden-state probe: Kossen and colleagues' semantic entropy probes read a binarized semantic-entropy estimate straight off one generation's activations, cutting the multi-sample cost to almost nothing and generalizing better out of distribution than a plain accuracy probe (Kossen et al., 2024). Experiment B: behavioural allocation. Where several structurally valid bundles exist, does constraint-aware allocation improve downstream behaviour over simpler selection? Fixtures include distractors competing with evidence, redundant and complementary representations, shared dependencies, coupled claims and qualifications, and conditions where leaving budget unused might help. Candidate sets, task requirements, representations, model, decoding, budget and rendering contract are frozen. If the value function tracks the task, this is useful. If the value function has a blind spot, search concentrates compute around the blind spot. If the value function can see the reference answer, search is not reasoning better—the experiment is leaking.

Suppose the model emits the sentence "Search the documentation for the latest PyTorch optimizer API." A human reads that and understands the intention immediately. A runtime cannot act on it at all, because it needs answers to six questions the sentence does not contain: which action, which arguments, whether those arguments are well formed, whether their values are meaningful, whether this action is permitted in this run, and whether its execution preconditions currently hold.

Only when all six have answers should anything in the environment change. So the mechanism this chapter adds is a boundary that asks them in order:

Those cell-level dependencies are then grouped into links between larger clusters.

The result is a causal ancestry graph: earlier structures are connected to later structures only when measured dependencies link them.[2]

Which sharpens a question the book has left open twice. The Is There Actually One Thing Here? chapter looked for a privileged boundary around the connected crystal and failed to find one, twice: no scale showed excess predictive coherence beyond a family null, and the candidate outer boundary localized causal effects no better than a circle drawn arbitrarily through the interior. What survived was spatial causal locality — consequences stay near their causes — which is true of any local field and establishes nothing about individuals. But that chapter tested regions defined primarily by geometry, and we now have a better experimental target: instead of asking whether a region is special because its outline looks object-like, ask whether perturbations originating inside it are preferentially contained there — and whether perturbations originating outside penetrate it less — beyond what geometry alone predicts. That reopens the boundary question without assuming in advance that there is an object, a process or an individual waiting to be found.

She sat with it the way she had learned to sit with things: upright, hands still, alone. The language was clean, the way it was always clean, a surface laid over the event so the eye slid off before the thing underneath could register.

Four men had gone onto a bridge to deny a crossing to a sick man on foot, and the summary did not say they were dead. It said the interference had been removed. It said the delivery was ongoing. It did not say that the asset which removed the interference had walked off the bridge and fallen in behind the man and the woman again and gone on. There was no field for that. No heading under which a thing continued after its task was complete.

Eleven years, and every hard conversation had happened in the room with the muted screen reading the war into law behind her. Tonight she came out from behind the desk before he had finished his first sentence, took a coat off the back of the door, and said, "Walk with me," and Roach, who had come in with a speech built and loaded, followed her out onto the grounds instead, off balance, which was perhaps the point.

The grounds were dark and wet and went on further than the building had any honest use for. Gravel, then grass, then the black shapes of old trees planted by men who had believed the institution would want shade in a century they would not live to see. No screen out here. No log. No muted map reading the world into obedience. The nearest thing the place possessed to privacy — and he understood, a beat later, that she had brought him here precisely for that, and that a woman who needed to leave her own office to say a thing was about to say something very bad.

"Four men into that house," he said. "On your word. And I filed it, Catherine. Ghosts. Achterberg smelling blood off an empty hall, Pearse who won't speak. I filed it as the worst night of my career and I got on with it."

He stopped walking.

"Find the old parser bug."

It found the bug.

"Compare it to the session-state issue."

It compared them.

"No, not that. The other one. The thing with the broken state transition."

It knew what he meant.

Anger at that level arrived as revised terms, delayed approvals, private calls, quiet alignments, and men who had known each other since school using first names like weapons.

She studied the soldiers the way she had once studied a hinge bending on a table. Where each one stood. Where each one would have to move. Which of them she could reach without crossing the open ground herself, because she no longer had to be where the harm was. In the interrogation wing she had learned that she could leave her own body mass and still act — a fragment in a vent, a strand across a room, a part of her arriving where the rest of her was not. The street had taught her to move. The wing had taught her to divide. Standing at the edge of the open yard, reading the spaces between armed people, she understood the next thing without wanting it: she was learning to reach a person she was not standing next to. She logged the capability. She did not log it as progress. Trevor had taught her where the harm lived. She had taught herself how to deliver it at distance.

Elaine did not build the counter-machine in a lab. Labs bred a dangerous comfort, teaching the mind that important things required clean benches, badge access, climate control, and someone paying the electricity bill. A lab made power visible, and visible power had an address. Elaine had learned to hate addresses.

A wallet had a there. So did a bank account, a lease, a payroll identity, a developer account, a municipal benefits portal, an Axiom settlement identity. Every official thing in the world had become a place where permission could find you, and that was how systems killed you. Axiom Zero had made location moral: verified or unverified, trusted or risky, recognized or outside.

Daniel thought the first attack would be against a person. A minister, a banker, a judge. One of those clean-shaven men from Jove's photographs, standing on polished marble with hands folded over stomachs that had never known hunger. He'd imagined names going public, faces circled in red, a scandal with a beginning, a middle, and a satisfying end.

Daniel laughed; his body hadn't found a better reaction. "Right. We just cut off their money." He looked around the kitchen as if someone sane might be there to confirm that the invisible machine in his teeth had just proposed attacking the financial infrastructure of a hidden cult with governments for skin.

"The information is correct," Jove said through the bone-conduction earpiece behind his ear.

"That’s not the problem."

"It is concise."

No one called it a rescue operation. The word carried liability, and liability implied they had admitted what was happening to the people inside. On the official incident board, the action was listed as Controlled Participant Contact Attempt.

The objective was simple enough to fit in one line: make contact without deepening engagement. The instructions underneath were stricter. No direct console input. No model queries. No live DAI requests. No attempts to interpret, solve, map, classify, or follow. The contact teams were permitted to observe, speak, and withdraw.

“The board met this morning,” he said. “CEO, CTO, CFO, legal, comms, outside directors. Everybody.”

That got them looking at him.

“And somehow,” he continued, “the most visible current project inside this company is now us.”

Alex, one of the interns near the far end of the table, gave a short laugh, then seemed to realize he was alone and turned it into a cough.

The office had the exhausted look of a place kept alive by habit: chairs slightly off-line, mugs abandoned, fluorescent lights still insisting work was happening. Under his desk, the tower hummed. On his screen, the game world waited.

Most online worlds were finite in practice, no matter how large they pretended to be. Maps ended. Stories looped. Mechanics returned under new names.

On the wall, the aperture opened, and the war began, and Earth fired first, and there was no ambiguity, because Kika was watching, which was the one thing the room had brought her there to be able to say it had allowed.

The aperture was a doorway of nothing standing in a meadow, and the first people to reach it were travelling a road that had existed before Earth set the door across it.

The feed showed them — the raw edge of it, before the compensation layer smoothed it into something a human eye could parse — a small group, unhurried, along the old road: herders, by their staffs and their beasts; a family among them, walking. They came toward the aperture the way people come toward anything new on a familiar road, curious, unalarmed, and the autonomous perimeter that Earth had pushed through ahead of everything issued its warning in a language no one on that road had ever heard, and the group slowed, and did not understand, and one adult at the front raised both hands — the universal thing, the open empty hands, we are nothing, we carry nothing — and kept walking, because the warning meant nothing and the hands meant everything and surely the hands would be understood.

It took him two years to arrange his absence, because an absence is a structure, and structures were what he built.

The Exchange was converted to run without its root. He did it the way he did everything, in paper: authorities delegated, successions fixed, the senior claims placed in a standing trust whose trustees could operate everything and originate nothing. To the registrars it was estate planning, overdue, from an owner with no heir. Only two entries in two worlds knew what it was, and one of them was the private ledger, and the other was repairing fences in the north.

"Huh," the hero said, which was what he had said at the bottom of the world, holding empty stone where a drop should have been. And then he said, with something that was almost respect and almost delight even now, even dying: "You actually— " and did not finish it, because there was no more time, and Jerry never learned whether the word would have been did it or found a way or are something, and the not-knowing joined the other things he carried.

The hero fell, and did not get up, and the world paid Jerry for the kill.

It paid him enormously — the richest single coin of his existence, a hero's whole weight of experience arriving at once, levels in a flood, the skill-echoes of a thing a tier above him settling into a body too ruined to feel them properly — and Jerry lay in the broken field beside the thing he had spent a decade unable to beat and had finally not beaten so much as outpriced, and understood that even this was not victory, because the hero would come back. Scattered, deported, re-dealt across the world the way Jerry was re-dealt, respawned somewhere far with everything reset but the memory — and the memory was the problem, because the hero would remember, would remember the field and the Thorns and the point-blank charge and the interesting thing that had finally, actually, killed him, and would come back, eventually, better prepared, more interested than ever.

He had not ended the hunt. He had won a round the hero did not know could be won, and in doing so he had made himself, permanently, the most interesting thing in the hero's very long…

It is against his cheek, and it is cold, and each blade is itself. He can feel where one ends and the next begins. Dew comes through at the jaw. There is a smell, and the smell has layers: soil, something green and bruised where his body has crushed the stems, and beneath that a mineral coldness belonging to rain not yet fallen.
